title: Warming up
hookLine: psalms before the main prayer, to prepare the heart
tomorrow: Blessed is the one who spoke

cards: No singer walks onstage cold. Backstage there are scales, humming, lip trills, the odd noises that loosen a voice. Runners jog before they run.
Even a hard conversation goes better after a minute to breathe in the car. The body and the heart both need a ramp. The Jewish morning service has one built in.
Before the Shema, before the standing prayer at its center, comes a long stretch of psalms and songs whose job, more or less, is to warm you up.

teach.b: It's called Pesukei d'Zimra, verses of song. It opens with a blessing, Baruch She'amar, closes with another, Yishtabach, and between them come psalms and passages of praise.

teach.h: AN HOUR TO DIRECT THE HEART.
teach.b: The Mishnah, in tractate Berakhot, remembers that the early pious ones would wait an hour before praying, to direct their hearts.

The Talmud adds a principle from Rabbi Simlai: always first set out the praise of God, and only then ask for anything. He learns it from Moses, who begins his plea with praise before asking to enter the land.

And in tractate Shabbat, Rabbi Yose says: may my portion be among those who complete the praise every day. The Talmud explains he meant these verses of song, the psalms near the end of the Book of Psalms.
So the order is deliberate. Thanks for waking, then a little study, then song, and only then the central prayers. Praise before asking.
Some teachers love a play on the word zimra.
The same three Hebrew letters can mean to sing and to prune, as you prune a vine.
So the verses of song can be heard as verses of pruning, cutting away distractions so the prayer can grow. That's wordplay, not the word's history, but some find it fits the experience.

how: Pesukei d'Zimra is said each morning between the morning blessings and the Shema, opening with Baruch She'amar and closing with Yishtabach; on Shabbat and festivals more psalms are added, and many communities sing parts of it aloud.

verses of song: psalms that warm up the heart
verses of mourning for the lost Temple

games.q: inside the verses of song — tap the pairs.

s: the verses of song are the central prayer of the service
they come first, to warm the heart before the Shema and the standing prayer.
the Talmud teaches to set out God's praise before asking for anything
Rabbi Simlai learns it from Moses.
the link between singing and pruning is the word's proven history
the letters overlap; reading it as pruning is a teacher's wordplay.

games.q: you're arranging a morning service. where do the songs of praise go?
o: before the main prayers, to prepare the heart.
games.why: praise comes first. the verses of song sit between the morning blessings and the Shema, a ramp into the central prayers.

practice: Close your mouth and let a low hum start in your chest, any note, and feel it buzz in your ribs and face as it rises and falls like a slow tune with no words.
If you know a melody from a prayer or a psalm, hum that; if not, anything gentle. Notice your breath lengthening and your shoulders softening.
